blocks.text:
Physical memory is a single, finite resource shared by every process, the kernel and the devices of a machine. If programs addressed that memory directly, three problems would follow immediately. A program could read or overwrite the memory of another program. A program would have to be compiled for the exact physical addresses it will occupy, which are unknown until it runs. The total size of all running programs could never exceed the installed RAM. Virtual memory removes all three problems with one mechanism: every process addresses a private, contiguous range of virtual addresses, and hardware together with the kernel translates each virtual address to a physical address on every access.

This chapter defines the mechanism, shows the layout of the address space of a small C program and of a JVM on the build machine, and explains how `malloc` and the JVM obtain memory from the kernel. The next chapter describes the translation hardware itself.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Definitions

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: The range of addresses a process can generate. On x86-64 Linux with 4-level paging the usable range is 48 bits: 128 TiB for user space (low half) and 128 TiB reserved for the kernel (high half). Each process has its own virtual address space; a virtual address has no meaning outside the process that generated it.

Physical memory is divided into fixed-size **frames** (4 KiB on x86-64) and the virtual address space into **pages** of the same size. A **page table** maps a virtual page number to a physical frame number. The memory management unit (MMU) of the CPU consults the page table of the running process on every instruction fetch, load and store. A page that has no valid mapping raises a **page fault**, a synchronous exception handled by the kernel.

blocks.text: #### What virtual memory provides

rows: Each process has its own page tables; a process cannot name a frame that is not mapped into its tables.
A program is linked once against virtual addresses; the kernel decides which frames back them.
The sum of the virtual sizes may exceed RAM; frames are assigned when a page is first touched.
The same frame may appear in several page tables: shared libraries, shared memory, the page cache.
Each page-table entry carries read, write, execute and user/supervisor bits enforced by the MMU.
Pages are created on first access (demand paging) or loaded from a file on first access.
blocks.caption: Services of virtual memory.

blocks.text:
#### Virtual memory areas

The kernel does not track individual pages of a process in one list. It records the address space as a set of **virtual** **memory areas** (VMAs). Each VMA is a contiguous range of pages with identical permissions and the same backing: anonymous (zero-filled, swap-backed) or a region of a file. The VMAs of a process are the lines of `/proc/PID/maps`. A page-table entry exists only for pages that were actually touched. The VMA answers the question "is this address legal and what should be there"; the page table answers "which frame holds it now".

Each line of `/proc/PID/maps` has the format `start-end perms offset device inode path`. The permission field has four characters: `r` read, `w` write, `x` execute and `p` private (copy-on-write) or `s` shared. A mapping with permissions `---p` reserves address space without allowing any access; the JVM uses it for memory that it has reserved but not yet committed.

#### Segments of a process image

rows: Memory obtained by `brk`; used by `malloc` for small blocks
Shared libraries, file mappings, large `malloc` blocks, thread stacks
Call frames, local variables of the main thread; limit `ulimit -s` (8192 KiB here)
Kernel-provided pages for fast system calls such as `clock_gettime`
blocks.caption: Standard regions of a Linux process.

blocks.text:
#### Address-space layout randomisation

With address-space layout randomisation (ASLR) the kernel adds a random offset to the base of the executable (for position-independent executables), the heap, the mmap area and the stack at every `exec`. Exploits that rely on fixed addresses therefore fail. The setting is `kernel.randomize_va_space`: 0 disables ASLR, 1 randomises stack, mmap and vdso, 2 also randomises the heap start. On the build machine the value is 2. Two consecutive runs of the same program below printed stack addresses `0x7fff2d3219f4` and `0x7ffff57c1fe4`; the heap start differed as well.

### Worked trace: the address space of a C program

The program below prints one address from each region and then dumps its own `/proc/PID/maps`.

blocks.title: layout.c
Compile and run (typical output; addresses differ on every run because of ASLR)

blocks.text:
The trace is read as follows.

1. `main` (`0x5623b6b5c249`) lies in the `r-xp` mapping `5623b6b5c000-5623b6b5d000`, the text segment of the executable. The string literal `msg` points into the following `r--p` page, the read-only data.
2. `global_init` (`...f010`) and `global_bss` (`...f040`) lie in the `rw-p` page starting at `...f000`. The executable occupies five consecutive VMAs at the low end of the address space (`0x5623...`, a randomised base for a position-independent executable).
3. `malloc(100)` returned `0x5623d23d22a0`, inside `[heap]` (`...d2000-...f3000`, 132 KiB = 0x21000 bytes). The heap starts at a random offset after the executable.
4. `malloc(1 << 20)` returned `0x7f7e58621010`, inside an anonymous 1 MiB + 4 KiB mapping at `7f7e58621000-7f7e58725000`. The 16 bytes before the returned address hold the allocator header. The explicit `mmap` returned the page-aligned `0x7f7e58300000`.
5. The libc mapping is split into four VMAs with different permissions: `r--p` headers, `r-xp` code, `r--p` read-only data, `rw-p` writable data. The file offset column shows which part of `libc.so.6` backs each VMA.
6. The stack VMA `7ffee011f000-7ffee0145000` is 152 KiB at this moment (0x26000 bytes). It grows downward on demand up to the `ulimit -s` limit of 8192 KiB. `local` (`0x7ffee013e074`) is near its upper end.
7. `[vdso]` and `[vvar]` are pages supplied by the kernel; the vDSO implements `clock_gettime` and `gettimeofday` without a system call. `[vsyscall]` is a legacy fixed page at the top of the address space.

blocks.text:
### How the heap and the mmap area grow

User space obtains virtual memory from the kernel with two system calls. `brk` moves the end of the **program break**, the upper boundary of the heap VMA. `mmap` creates an arbitrary new VMA. The C library allocator (`malloc` in glibc) uses `brk` for small requests and `mmap` for requests above a threshold (128 KiB by default, adjusted dynamically up to 32 MiB). The allocator also keeps per-thread arenas, each a reserved 64 MiB region, to reduce lock contention in multithreaded programs; this is the origin of the many `---p` regions in a JVM, described later.

blocks.text: The system calls of a program that performs `malloc(100)`, `malloc(1 << 20)` and frees both can be observed directly.

blocks.code:
$ strace -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap ./mal 2>&1 | tail -4
brk(NULL)                               = 0x56495da2f000
brk(0x56495da50000)                     = 0x56495da50000
mmap(NULL, 1052672, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7f2b63aff000
munmap(0x7f2b63aff000, 1052672)         = 0
blocks.title: Trace brk, mmap and munmap of mal.c (loader calls omitted)

blocks.text:
The first `brk(NULL)` queries the current break. The second call extends it by 0x21000 bytes (132 KiB), which provides the arena for `malloc(100)`. The 1 MiB request exceeds the mmap threshold and becomes a separate mapping of 1052672 bytes (1 MiB plus one page for the header). `free` of the large block calls `munmap`, so the resident set drops immediately; `free` of a small block normally keeps the memory in the arena for reuse, which is why the resident size of a long-running C or native-library process rarely shrinks.

### Hands-on: the address space of a JVM

A JVM is an ordinary process; its address space contains the same regions plus areas that the JVM reserves for its own purposes. The program `Idle.java` allocates 100 MiB of live arrays and a 16 MiB direct buffer and then sleeps. It was started with `java -Xmx256m -Xms64m -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` (default G1 collector on this 2-CPU, 8 GiB machine; the JDK is OpenJDK 21.0.12).

$ wc -l < /proc/1777/maps
182
$ grep -E "^(VmPeak|VmSize|VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile|VmData|VmStk|Threads)" /proc/1777/status

VmSize:  2868616 kB
VmRSS:    162952 kB

blocks.title: Size and shape of the JVM address space (PID 1777, typical output)

blocks.text: The process has 182 VMAs, a virtual size of 2.74 GiB and a resident set of 159 MiB. The virtual size is 17.6 times the resident size, which is normal for a JVM. The large regions, listed by the script below, explain it.

blocks.code:
import sys

# Print the VMAs of a process that are at least 8 MiB, and the total of the reserved (---p) ones.
reserved = 0
for line in open("/proc/%s/maps" % sys.argv[1]):
    f = line.split()
    start, end = (int(x, 16) for x in f[0].split("-"))
    kb = (end - start) // 1024
    if f[1] == "---p":
        reserved += kb
    if kb >= 8192:
        print(f[0], f[1], "%d KB" % kb, f[5] if len(f) > 5 else "")
print(reserved, "KB reserved, no access")

blocks.title: Regions of 8 MiB or more in /proc/1777/maps (selected lines of the real output)

blocks.text:
The regions are, in order: the committed part of the Java heap, its reserved remainder, the 1 GiB compressed class space, the mapped JDK class image, the VM library itself, the class-data-sharing archive, a reservation of the code cache, and one of the 64 MiB malloc arenas.

Three observations follow. First, the Java heap starts at `0xf0000000` and its reserved size is exactly `-Xmx256m` (0xf0000000 to 0x100000000). The heap ends exactly at the 4 GiB boundary (0x100000000), which allows the JVM to use compressed object pointers without any base or shift (32-bit references). Second, `---p` regions occupy more than 2 GiB of virtual size but consume no frames and no swap; they are reservations. The 1 GiB compressed class space is reserved once at start-up and committed in small pieces as classes load. Third, the JDK class image `lib/modules` is mapped read-only and shared; its pages enter the resident set (RssFile) only when classes are read from it, and they can be dropped and re-read at any time because they are backed by a file.

The system also contains the JVM threads: `ls /proc/1777/task | wc -l` gave 19 during the run (20 after `jcmd` attached). Each is a Linux task with its own stack VMA; the next chapters of this part and the following part treat them.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: alert on virtual memory size of a Java service

**Scenario.** A monitoring template for a fleet of Spring Boot services raises a warning when `VSZ` (virtual size) of a process exceeds 1.5 times the container memory limit. A service with `-Xmx256m` in a 512 MiB container is reported with a virtual size of 2.8 GiB and the alert fires on every instance, although the services are healthy.

**Symptoms.** The alert dashboard shows `VmSize` of 2.8 GiB against a 512 MiB limit. No restarts, no `OutOfMemoryError`, no kernel OOM messages occur. Resident size stays near 160 MiB.

**Diagnosis.** The two sizes are compared directly, then the large regions are listed by permission.

blocks.code:
$ grep -E "VmSize|VmRSS" /proc/1777/status
VmSize:  2868616 kB
VmRSS:    162952 kB
$ python3 bigmaps.py 1777 | tail -1
2471884 KB reserved, no access
blocks.title: Compare virtual and resident size, then total the reservations (PID 1777)

blocks.text:
The `---p` regions (heap tail, class space, code cache, arenas) total 2.36 GiB, most of the 2.74 GiB virtual size. The `VmSize` metric counts address space, not memory. Neither the kernel limit nor the OOM killer considers it: a memory cgroup limits resident pages (anonymous, page cache and kernel memory charged to the cgroup), and a limit on address space exists only if `ulimit -v` or `RLIMIT_AS` is set.

**Root cause.** The alert uses a metric that measures reservation instead of consumption.

**Fix.** Immediate: silence the rule for JVM processes. Permanent: alert on resident memory (`VmRSS`, `container_memory_working_set_bytes` in Kubernetes) relative to the container limit, and on the NMT committed total when a finer view is required.

**Prevention.** Document in the monitoring standard that virtual size is informational. Review any use of `ulimit -v` for JVMs: a limit smaller than the reservations (about 1.25 GiB for the class space and code cache alone) prevents the JVM from starting.

#### Incident: JVM fails to start with a low virtual-memory limit

**Scenario.** A hardening script sets `ulimit -v 1000000` (about 1 GB) before starting a service to prevent runaway memory use.

**Symptoms.** The JVM exits during start-up with `Error occurred during initialization of VM` and a message that it could not reserve enough space for the object heap or the compressed class space. **Diagnosis.** The limit is verified and the minimum reservation estimated from the maps of a running JVM.

blocks.code:
$ (ulimit -v 1000000; java -Xmx256m -version 2>&1 | grep -v Picked)
Error occurred during initialization of VM
Could not allocate compressed class space: 1073741824 bytes
$ (ulimit -v 3000000; java -Xmx256m -version 2>&1 | grep -v Picked | head -1)
openjdk version "21.0.12.1" 2026-08-18
blocks.title: Reproduction with a virtual-memory limit of about 1 GB, then 3 GB

blocks.text:
The failing reservation is the 1 GiB compressed class space; the message names the first reservation that does not fit, and the exact text can differ between JDK builds.

**Root cause.** `RLIMIT_AS` limits the total size of all VMAs, including the `---p` reservations; the JVM reserves the 1 GiB class space and the code cache before running any user code.

**Fix.** Remove `ulimit -v` and limit memory with a cgroup (`MemoryMax=` in a systemd unit, or the container limit), which accounts for resident pages.

**Prevention.** Test every start-up wrapper with the real JVM flags in a pre-production environment.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is the difference between a virtual address and a physical address?** A virtual address is generated by a process and is translated by the MMU through the page tables of that process to a physical address, which identifies a byte of RAM. Two processes can use the same virtual address for different data.
2. **Why do the virtual sizes of Java processes exceed the heap size by gigabytes?** The JVM reserves address space (class space, code cache, heap up to `-Xmx`, per-thread arenas and stacks) without committing it. Reserved pages have no page-table entries and use no RAM.
3. **What is a VMA?** A virtual memory area is a contiguous range of pages with the same permissions and backing; the kernel keeps VMAs in a tree to validate addresses on page faults. `/proc/PID/maps` lists them.
4. **How do** `brk` **and** `mmap` **differ?** `brk` moves the end of the single heap segment; `mmap` creates an independent mapping anywhere in the address space and can be unmapped separately, which allows `free` to return large blocks to the kernel.
5. **What does ASLR protect against and what does it cost?** It makes the addresses of code, stack and heap unpredictable per run, which hinders exploits that jump to known addresses. The cost is negligible; position-independent code needs one extra register on 32-bit x86 and has little overhead on x86-64.
6. **Why does the resident size of a process not shrink after** `free`**?** Small blocks stay in the allocator arena for reuse; only whole top-of-heap regions or `mmap`-allocated blocks are returned.
7. **What does a mapping with permissions** `---p` **mean?** A reserved range with no access rights. Touching it raises `SIGSEGV`; the JVM later changes the permissions with `mprotect` or `mmap` to commit it.
8. **A segmentation fault occurs. What does the kernel actually do?** The access hits an address without a VMA or violates the VMA permissions. The page-fault handler cannot resolve it and sends `SIGSEGV` to the thread.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Virtual memory gives each process a private address space translated page by page by the MMU.

- The kernel records the address space as VMAs (`/proc/PID/maps`); page-table entries exist only for touched pages.
- `brk` extends the heap; `mmap` creates all other regions; `malloc` uses both.
- ASLR randomises the base addresses at every `exec`; compare two runs to verify it.
- A JVM reserves far more address space than it uses; judge consumption by resident size and NMT, not by `VmSize`.
- A `---p` mapping reserves addresses without frames; `RLIMIT_AS` counts these reservations.

A virtual address is useless until it is translated to a physical address. Translation must be fast, because it happens for every instruction fetch and every memory operand, and it must be compact, because a map of 2^48 bytes of address space cannot be stored as a flat table. Paging solves both requirements with a hierarchy of small tables and a cache of recent translations. This chapter derives the structure, performs a complete translation with real values, measures page faults with a C program, and relates the results to the JVM.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Why a flat page table is impossible

With 4 KiB pages a 48-bit address contains a 36-bit virtual page number. A flat table with one 8-byte entry per page would need 2^36 × 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, almost all of it describing unused addresses. A multi-level table allocates a lower-level table only if some address below it is in use. A process whose mappings occupy a few hundred megabytes needs a few hundred kilobytes of page tables.

#### The four-level structure

On x86-64, the 48 bits of a virtual address are split into four 9-bit indices and a 12-bit offset. Each table is exactly one 4 KiB page holding 512 entries of 8 bytes.

blocks.text:
The register `CR3` holds the physical address of the PGD of the running process. A context switch to another process loads a different `CR3`. Linux 6.x can also be built with five levels (a P4D level between PGD and PUD) for 57-bit address spaces; the default user address space remains 47 bits.

#### The page-table entry

An entry is 64 bits. The low bits carry control flags and the middle bits carry the physical frame number (PFN). The flags relevant for the operating system are: **P** (present), **R/W** (writable), **U/S** (accessible from user mode), **A** (accessed, set by hardware on any access), **D** (dirty, set by hardware on a write), **PS** (page size: the entry maps a huge page) and **NX** (no execute). The kernel reads **A** and **D** to decide which pages to evict and which must be written back. If **P** is zero the remaining bits are free for the kernel; Linux stores a swap location or a file offset there.

blocks.caption: The 64-bit page-table entry: the frame number occupies bits 51..12; present, writable, user, accessed, dirty, page-size and no-execute flags control the access.
blocks.alt: x86-64 page-table entry (64 bits, 8 bytes) | 63 32 | NX software / ignored PFN bits 51..32 | 31 0 | PFN bits 31..12 (physical frame number) avail G PS D A PCD PWT U/S R/W P | P present, R/W writable, U/S user-accessible, A accessed, D dirty, PS huge page, NX no-execute

blocks.text:
#### The translation lookaside buffer

A walk costs four dependent memory reads. The CPU therefore caches complete translations in the **translation** **lookaside buffer** (TLB). The TLB is indexed by the virtual page number (and an address-space tag, the PCID on x86) and stores the frame number and permissions. A hit adds almost no latency. A miss starts the hardware page walker, which reads the page tables through the normal data caches; page-table entries of recently used regions are usually in the L1 or L2 cache, so most walks cost far less than four main-memory accesses.

blocks.text:
The **TLB reach** is the number of entries multiplied by the page size. The sizes vary by CPU model and are available from `cpuid`; a typical recent Intel core has a first-level data TLB of 64 entries and a second-level TLB of 1,024 to 2,048 entries (these figures are typical and not measured here). With 4 KiB pages 1,536 entries cover 6 MiB; with 2 MiB pages the same number of entries covers 3 GiB. A process that randomly touches more memory than its TLB reach spends a measurable part of its time in page walks. A context switch changes the address space; the PCID tag lets the TLB keep entries of several address spaces and avoids a full flush.

#### Effective access time

If the TLB hit ratio is h, the TLB lookup costs t and a memory access costs m, a translation that hits costs t + m for the access. On a miss the walk performs four additional memory reads before the data access: t + 4m + m. The effective access time is therefore h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 5m).

#### Huge pages

Setting the PS bit in a PMD entry maps 2 MiB with a single entry and no PTE level; a PUD entry can map 1 GiB. Benefits: one TLB entry covers 512 times as much memory, the walk is one level shorter and the number of page faults falls. Costs: a fault must zero 2 MiB, a partly used huge page wastes memory, and a free 2 MiB contiguous region is needed, which may require compaction. Linux offers two mechanisms: explicit huge pages reserved with `vm.nr_hugepages` (used through `hugetlbfs` or `MAP_HUGETLB`) and **transparent huge pages** (THP), where the kernel promotes regions automatically. The system setting is `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` with the values `always`, `madvise` and `never`; this machine reports `madvise`, so only regions that call `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` are eligible.

#### Page faults

A page fault is raised by the MMU when a translation fails: the entry is not present, or the access violates the entry permissions. The kernel handler classifies the fault by looking up the VMA that contains the address.

rows: Address in no VMA, or access not permitted by the VMA
First touch of an anonymous page
Allocate a zeroed frame, map it
Page is in the page cache but not mapped
Page is not in the cache
Read it from the file, then map it (task sleeps)
Read from the swap device, then map
Write to a present, write-protected private page
Copy the frame, map the copy writable
blocks.caption: Classification of page faults.

blocks.text: A **minor** fault is resolved without disk I/O; a **major** fault requires it. Both are counted per process (`min_flt` and `maj_flt` in `/proc/PID/stat`, `ru_minflt` and `ru_majflt` in `getrusage`).

blocks.text:
#### Demand paging

When `exec` or `mmap` creates a mapping, no frames are allocated and no data is read. The first access to each page faults, and the handler supplies the page. A 64 MiB anonymous mapping that is never touched costs nothing; a 1 GiB executable that executes only a fraction of its code loads only that fraction. The price is a fault at the first access of every page. The sequence for a major fault on a file-backed page is shown below.

blocks.text:
#### Copy-on-write

`fork` must give the child a copy of the address space of the parent. Copying every page would be wasteful because most children call `exec` immediately. Linux copies only the page tables and marks all private writable pages read-only in both processes; the frames are shared and their reference counts are increased. The first write by either process faults. The handler allocates a new frame, copies the 4 KiB, updates the writer's entry to point to the copy with write permission, and decrements the reference count of the original. The same mechanism makes the all-zero page, shared libraries mapped privately, and snapshots by `fork` in databases efficient.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace: translating 0x555e4c6c93c3

The program `walk.c` allocates memory, forces a page into existence, splits an address into its table indices and asks the kernel for the real frame number through `/proc/self/pagemap` (readable by root; unprivileged users receive zero frame numbers).

blocks.title: walk.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o walk walk.c && ./walk
virtual address   0x0000555e4c6c93c3
bits 47..39 (PGD) 170
bits 38..30 (PUD) 377
bits 29..21 (PMD) 99
bits 20..12 (PTE) 201
bits 11..0  (off) 0x3c3
pagemap entry     0x8100000000141c7c
present=1 swapped=0 soft-dirty=0 exclusive=1 pfn=0x141c7c
physical address  0x141c7c3c3
blocks.title: Run walk.c (typical output; the address and the frame number differ on every run)

blocks.text:
The binary form of the 48 low bits is `010101010 101111001 001100011 011001001 001111000011`, which gives the indices 170, 377, 99 and 201 and the offset `0x3c3`. The hardware performs these steps.

1. Read `CR3`: the physical address of the PGD of the process.
2. PGD: read the 8-byte entry at byte offset 170 × 8 = 0x550. It is present and holds the physical address of a PUD table.
3. PUD: read the entry at offset 377 × 8 = 0xBC8. It points to a PMD table.
4. PMD: read the entry at offset 99 × 8 = 0x318. The PS bit is zero, so it points to a PTE table.
5. PTE: read the entry at offset 201 × 8 = 0x648. It holds the frame number `0x141c7c` with the present, writable and user bits set. The kernel exposes this entry through the pagemap file as `0x8100000000141c7c`: bit 63 (present) and bit 56 (exclusively mapped) are set, and bits 54..0 hold the frame number.
6. Physical address = (`0x141c7c` \<\< 12) | `0x3c3` = `0x141c7c3c3`.
7. The TLB stores the pair (virtual page `0x555e4c6c9`, frame `0x141c7c`); the next access to any byte of this page needs no walk.

blocks.text:
The table assumes that all four page-table reads miss every cache; in practice they usually hit the cache hierarchy and the penalty is smaller. The conclusion remains: translation cost depends on the TLB hit ratio, and the working set of a program should fit within the TLB reach where possible.

### Hands-on: measuring page faults

#### Faults per page and copy-on-write

The program `faults.c` counts the faults of the current process with `getrusage` around each action.

blocks.title: faults.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -o faults faults.c && (ulimit -v 600000; ./faults)
anonymous 64 MiB mapped, no page touched: +0 minor
write one byte per page (16384 pages):      +16384 minor
write the same pages again:                 +0 minor
file 32 MiB, cache cold, read each page:  +260 minor, +1 major
file 32 MiB, cache warm, read each page:  +260 minor, +0 major
file cold, MADV_RANDOM, 1000 pages:       +0 minor, +1000 major
child writes 4096 inherited pages (COW):  +4096 minor
child reads 4096 inherited pages:         +0 minor
blocks.title: Run faults.c under a 600 MB address-space limit (typical output)

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- Mapping 64 MiB costs no fault. Writing one byte to each of the 16,384 pages costs exactly 16,384 minor faults. A second pass costs none, because the entries are now present.
- Reading a cold 32 MiB file through `mmap` caused one major fault and 260 minor faults, not 8,192 faults. The kernel reads ahead around the faulting page and its fault-around logic maps neighbouring pages that are already in the page cache in a single fault. After eviction with `posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)` the first access paid disk I/O once; the remaining requests were served from the read-ahead window.
- With `MADV_RANDOM` (no read-ahead, no fault-around) each of 1,000 distinct pages produced one major fault, which is the worst case for a database or an index that is accessed randomly.
- The child that wrote to 4,096 inherited pages took 4,096 minor faults, each including a 4 KiB copy. The child that only read took none, because the page-table entries were copied at `fork`.

#### Faults of a JVM heap

The following run starts a JVM with a 256 MiB heap and `-version`, with and without `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch`, which writes to every heap page during start-up. Fault counts were read from `getrusage` of the child process.

blocks.code:
$ python3 pretouch.py
-Xms256m -Xmx256m                            0.07 s  minor faults   4754
-Xms256m -Xmx256m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch        0.29 s  minor faults  73150
-Xms256m -Xmx256m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch THP    0.29 s  minor faults   4890
blocks.title: Minor faults and start-up time (measured on the build machine, typical)

blocks.text:
(The third line adds `-XX:+UseTransparentHugePages`; it was 0.19 s in a second run, so the timing is noisy.) A start without pre-touch takes about 4,750 faults, mostly for the JVM and library images. Pre-touching 256 MiB adds about 68,400 faults, which is 65,536 heap pages plus some auxiliary structures, and multiplies the start-up time by about four. With transparent huge pages the extra faults disappear (4,890 in total), because the 256 MiB heap is mapped by huge pages.

#### Transparent huge pages

blocks.title: thp.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -o thp thp.c && (ulimit -v 400000; ./thp)
default (madvise mode):   8194 faults, AnonHugePages      0 kB, first touch 28.6 ms
MADV_HUGEPAGE         :     16 faults, AnonHugePages  32768 kB, first touch 15.3 ms
blocks.title: Run thp.c under a 400 MB address-space limit (typical output)

blocks.text: The same 32 MiB took 8,194 faults of 4 KiB in the default configuration and 16 faults of 2 MiB with `MADV_HUGEPAGE`; `AnonHugePages` in `/proc/self/smaps_rollup` confirms that all 32 MiB were mapped by huge pages. Per-fault cost is about 2 to 3.5 microseconds for a 4 KiB page and about 1 millisecond for a 2 MiB page (dominated by zeroing 2 MiB). The total first-touch time is similar; the benefit appears later as fewer TLB misses, the cost as longer individual faults.

blocks.text:
#### TLB and cache effects

The program `tlb.c` (not listed) builds a random cyclic list in which every element lies on a different page and chases it for 20 million steps. It reports the time per step as the number of pages grows.

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -o tlb tlb.c && (ulimit -v 300000; ./tlb)
pages  working set  ns per access
    16      64 KiB     3.1
    64     256 KiB     2.6
   256    1024 KiB     5.0
  1024    4096 KiB     8.4
  4096   16384 KiB    18.2
 16384   65536 KiB    39.3
blocks.title: Pointer chase over N pages, one cache line per page (measured, typical)

blocks.text: The time per access rises from 2.6 ns to 39.3 ns, a factor of 15, although the program executes the same instructions. The increase combines two effects that the program does not separate: the data no longer fits in the caches, and the translations no longer fit in the TLB. The measurement shows why the layout and the size of the working set matter even when no page fault occurs.

blocks.text: #### Observing faults of a live process

blocks.code:
$ awk '{print "minflt=" $10, "majflt=" $12}' /proc/self/stat
minflt=110 majflt=0
$ grep -E "^(pgfault|pgmajfault|thp_fault_alloc|thp_fault_fallback|compact_stall) " /proc/vmstat
pgfault 8507769
pgmajfault 325506
compact_stall 0
thp_fault_alloc 304
thp_fault_fallback 0
blocks.title: Fault counters of a process and of the system

blocks.text:
The fields 10 and 12 of `/proc/PID/stat` are the minor and major fault counters of the process; `/proc/vmstat` contains system-wide totals (`pgfault`, `pgmajfault`). A rising `pgmajfault` on a server that should be serving from memory is the primary sign of memory pressure.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: latency spikes from transparent huge page compaction

**Scenario.** A latency-sensitive Spring Boot service with a 4 GiB heap runs on a VM image whose THP setting was changed to `always` and defragmentation to `direct compaction` by a performance-tuning script. After several days of uptime the 99.9th percentile latency shows isolated stalls of 100 ms to several seconds.

**Symptoms.** Latency histograms show periodic outliers unrelated to request size. GC logs show pauses with a high system time (`sys=`) component. CPU profiles show time in `compact_zone` or `khugepaged`.

**Diagnosis.** The THP policy and activity counters are read first.

blocks.code:
$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
always [madvise] never
$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag
always defer defer+madvise [madvise] never
$ grep -E "^(thp_fault_alloc|thp_fault_fallback|compact_stall) " /proc/vmstat
compact_stall 0
thp_fault_alloc 304
thp_fault_fallback 0
blocks.title: THP configuration and counters (build machine values; the stall counters are the ones to watch)

blocks.text:
On the build machine the settings are conservative and `compact_stall` is 0. On the affected host the combination `enabled = always` and `defrag = always` with a rising `compact_stall` and `thp_fault_fallback` indicates that page faults wait for memory compaction because no free 2 MiB block is available; the counters are cumulative since boot, so the growth rate between two samples is what matters.

**Root cause.** With `defrag = always` a fault that cannot find a free huge page compacts memory synchronously in the context of the application thread. Fragmentation grows with uptime and the page cache, so the problem appears only after days.

**Fix.** Immediate: `echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` and `echo defer+madvise >` `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag` (as root; both take effect at once). Permanent: persist the setting in the image (kernel command line `transparent_hugepage=madvise` or a systemd unit) and, if the JVM benefits from huge pages, enable `-XX:+UseTransparentHugePages` together with `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` so that the pages are obtained at start-up, not on the request path.

**Prevention.** Alert on the growth rate of `compact_stall`. Many database vendors (Redis, MongoDB, Oracle) recommend `madvise` or `never`; follow the guidance of each product.

#### Incident: slow first requests after a deployment

**Scenario.** After each rolling deployment of a service with `-Xms256m -Xmx2g`, the first minutes show elevated latency while the service is already receiving traffic. Warm-up runs of the load balancer are short.

**Symptoms.** CPU system time is high during the first minutes; the minor fault rate of the new process is in the tens of thousands per second; the latency falls without any change.

**Diagnosis.** The fault rate is sampled from the process counters.

blocks.code:
$ while [ -d /proc/$PID ]; do \
    awk '{print "minflt=" $10 " majflt=" $12}' /proc/$PID/stat; sleep 2; done
minflt=10283 majflt=0
minflt=21232 majflt=0
minflt=31497 majflt=0
minflt=41814 majflt=0
minflt=52139 majflt=0
blocks.title: Fault rate of a JVM whose live heap grows by 20 MiB per second (reproduction, Grow.java)

blocks.text:
The counter rises by about 10,300 every two seconds: 5,120 pages per 20 MiB step, which is one minor fault per newly used 4 KiB page. A heap that grows from 256 MiB to 2 GiB commits new pages as the allocation front advances. At 2 to 3.5 microseconds per first touch (measured above), 1.75 GiB of new heap means about 460,000 faults and roughly one to two seconds of CPU time spread over the warm-up.

**Root cause.** Lazy commit of the heap by demand paging, combined with a start-up traffic burst.

**Fix.** Set `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` for steady services so that the heap does not resize, and use `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` when start-up time is acceptable (measured above: 0.07 s to 0.29 s for 256 MiB; it scales with the heap size, about 1 s per GiB on this machine). Use a readiness probe that opens only after warm-up requests.

**Prevention.** Measure start-up time with and without pre-touch before enabling it for large heaps: extrapolating the measured rate of about 1 second per GiB, pre-touching a 32 GiB heap can take about half a minute and may exceed the liveness probe timeout of the orchestrator.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **Why are page tables multi-level?** A single-level table for a 48-bit space needs 512 GiB per process. A multi-level table creates lower-level tables only for ranges in use, so a process pays for its mappings, not for the whole address space.
2. **Walk through the translation of a virtual address on x86-64.** Split the address into four 9-bit indices and a 12-bit offset. Starting at the PGD whose address is in `CR3`, each entry selects the next table; the PTE yields the frame number; the physical address is frame × 4096 + offset. The TLB caches the result.
3. **What is the TLB and what happens on a context switch?** A cache of virtual-to-physical translations. Without tags it is flushed on a switch; with PCID the entries of several address spaces coexist, and only changed entries need invalidation.
4. **What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?** A minor fault is resolved from memory (zero-fill, page cache hit, copy-on-write); a major fault needs I/O from a file or from swap and the task sleeps.
5. **How does** `fork` **avoid copying memory?** It copies the page tables, marks private pages read-only and shares the frames; the first write faults and the kernel copies that single page (copy-on-write).
6. **What is demand paging and why does** `mmap` **of a large file return immediately?** Mapping creates only a VMA; pages are read on first access. The cost is paid at the faults.
7. **When would you use huge pages, and what are the risks?** For large, long-lived heaps and databases with TLB-bound access patterns. Risks are memory bloat, compaction stalls and longer individual faults.
8. **A process shows** `maj_flt` **rising quickly. What does it mean?** The process is repeatedly reading pages that are not in memory: a cold file cache, a working set larger than available memory, or swapping. Check `vmstat` (`si`, `so`, `bi`) and `/proc/pressure/memory`.
9. **What happens on a write to a page mapped read-only?** If the VMA allows writing (copy-on-write or a page tracked for dirtiness), the kernel makes the page writable or copies it and resumes; otherwise `SIGSEGV` is sent.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Paging translates virtual to physical addresses with a four-level tree of 4 KiB tables and caches results in the TLB.

- A 48-bit address is four 9-bit indices plus a 12-bit offset; `CR3` locates the root table.
- The effective access time depends on the TLB hit ratio; working sets beyond the TLB reach cost time even without faults.
- Page faults are minor (no I/O) or major (I/O); first touch of anonymous memory costs one minor fault per 4 KiB page (measured 2 to 3.5 microseconds).
- Copy-on-write lets `fork` share frames; a child writing 4,096 inherited pages caused 4,096 faults in the measurement.
- Transparent huge pages reduce faults and TLB misses but can cause compaction stalls; the setting `madvise` is the conservative default.

sections.title: Page Replacement, Working Sets and Swapping

blocks.text:
Physical memory is smaller than the sum of the virtual memory in use. When a page fault needs a frame and no frame is free, the kernel must evict a resident page. The choice of the victim decides how many future faults occur. A good choice removes a page that will not be needed soon; a bad choice removes a page that is needed immediately, and the system spends its time moving pages between memory and disk instead of running programs. This chapter compares the classical algorithms on reference strings with verified counts, explains the working-set model and thrashing, and describes how Linux reclaims memory and uses swap.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The replacement problem

A **reference string** is the sequence of page numbers accessed by a program. With *n* frames the memory holds at most *n* pages. A reference to a resident page is a hit; a reference to a non-resident page is a page fault. If all frames are in use, the algorithm chooses a victim. The goal is to minimise the number of faults. A **dirty** page (modified since it was loaded) must be written to its backing store before the frame is reused, which makes evicting clean pages cheaper.

rows: Evict the page whose next use lies farthest in the future
Optimal; needs knowledge of the future; used as a yardstick
Evict the page that has been resident longest
Simple; ignores use; suffers Belady's anomaly
Evict the page unused for the longest time
Good approximation of OPT; exact LRU needs a timestamp or list update on every access
A hand sweeps a circular list; a page with reference bit 1 gets the bit cleared, a page with 0 is evicted
Approximates LRU using the hardware accessed bit
Classes by (referenced, modified); evict from the lowest non-empty class
Cheap; the bits are cleared periodically
Evict the least frequently used page
Old frequent pages stay too long without ageing
blocks.caption: Classical replacement algorithms.

blocks.text:
#### Belady's anomaly

Intuition says that more frames cannot cause more faults. For FIFO this is false. On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO produces 9 faults with three frames and 10 faults with four frames. The cause is that FIFO does not have the **stack** **property**: the set of pages resident with *n* frames is not always a subset of the set resident with *n+1* frames. LRU and OPT do have this property, so their fault count never rises when frames are added.

blocks.text:
#### The clock algorithm

Maintaining exact LRU order would require updating a list on every memory access, which is impossible in software because ordinary loads and stores do not trap. The hardware sets the **accessed bit** in the page-table entry for free. The clock algorithm uses it: the resident pages form a circle with a hand. When a victim is needed, the hand examines the page it points to. If the bit is 1, the page was used since the last sweep, so the bit is cleared and the hand advances (the page gets a second chance). If the bit is 0, the page is evicted and replaced by the new page, which enters with its bit set.

blocks.text:
#### Working sets and thrashing

The **working set** W(t, Δ) of a process is the set of pages it referenced during the last Δ memory references. A process runs efficiently if its working set is resident. If the sum of the working sets of all runnable processes exceeds the number of frames, every process faults continuously: each fault evicts a page that another process (or the same one) needs next. The CPU waits for the disk, CPU utilisation falls, and a scheduler that reacts to low utilisation by starting more processes makes the situation worse. This collapse is **thrashing**.

blocks.text:
Remedies are to reduce the degree of multiprogramming (suspend or swap out whole processes), to add memory, or to reduce the working set (a smaller heap, a smaller data structure, a better access pattern). A page-fault-frequency policy gives a process more frames when its fault rate is above an upper threshold and takes frames away below a lower one.

#### Reclaim in Linux

Linux does not run FIFO or pure clock. Anonymous and file-backed pages are kept on **active** and **inactive** lists per memory zone and per cgroup. A page enters the inactive list; if it is referenced again while on that list it moves to the active list; when the active list becomes too large, its oldest pages are demoted. Reclaim scans the inactive list: clean file pages are dropped, dirty file pages are written back first, anonymous pages are written to swap (if swap exists) and then freed. Newer kernels (6.1 and later) can replace this with a multi-generational LRU (`CONFIG_LRU_GEN`); the build machine kernel does not expose `/sys/kernel/mm/lru_gen`, so the classical lists are in use.

Reclaim runs in two contexts. The background thread `kswapd` wakes when free memory falls below the low watermark and works until the high watermark is reached. If an allocation cannot be satisfied, the allocating task performs **direct** **reclaim** itself and waits; this is where applications observe memory pressure as latency.

blocks.text:
#### Swap and swappiness

**Swap space** is a partition or file that holds anonymous pages that have no other backing store. Without swap, the kernel can reclaim only file-backed pages; anonymous memory can be freed only by killing processes. The parameter `vm.swappiness` (0 to 200 on current kernels, default 60) sets the relative cost of reclaiming anonymous pages compared with file pages: values near 0 make the kernel prefer dropping file cache; high values make it swap anonymous pages earlier to keep file cache. Each memory cgroup has its own `memory.swappiness`. The value 0 does not disable swapping; it avoids it until memory is nearly exhausted.

**zram** is a compressed block device in RAM used as swap. Pages that are swapped out are compressed and stored in memory, which costs CPU time but no disk I/O and typically saves memory when the data compresses well. It is often enabled on small machines and desktops.

On servers, swap has two conflicting effects. It allows inactive anonymous pages (for example, an idle part of a heap) to leave memory, which leaves more room for the page cache. It also converts memory exhaustion into severe slowdowns instead of a quick kill, because a swapped-out heap region must be read back when the garbage collector or the application touches it. Container platforms often run with swap disabled, so that a memory limit produces a clear OOM kill instead of slow thrashing.

What to notice:

- String A with FIFO reproduces the anomaly: 9 faults with three frames, 10 with four. Clock, which behaves like FIFO on this string, shows it as well (9 and 10).
- LRU on string A is worse than FIFO with three frames (10 against 9) although it is better with four frames (8). No online algorithm wins on every string; the guarantee of LRU is the stack property, not a lower count on each input.
- OPT is the lower bound in every row: 7 and 6 for string A, 9 and 8 for string B. On string B with three frames the ordering is OPT 9, LRU 12, Clock 14, FIFO 15, which is the usual ranking.

#### Thrashing in a memory cgroup

The program `thrash.c` maps a file of a given size and performs 300,000 random reads of one byte each through the mapping, with `MADV_RANDOM` so that no read-ahead hides the effect. It was run in a memory cgroup with a 40 MiB limit and without swap. A file-backed working set is used so that eviction does not kill the process: the kernel simply drops and re-reads clean pages. A fresh file was created for each run.

blocks.code:
$ for ws in 16 32 48 64; do rm -f ws.bin; ./thrash $ws; done
working set  16 MiB: 300000 random reads in   0.04 s, major faults   4096, minor     74
working set  32 MiB: 300000 random reads in   0.07 s, major faults   8192, minor     74
working set  48 MiB: 300000 random reads in   0.57 s, major faults  60595, minor     76
working set  64 MiB: 300000 random reads in   0.54 s, major faults 120062, minor     75
blocks.title: Random reads in a 40 MiB memory cgroup (measured, typical)

blocks.text: When the working set fits (16 and 32 MiB) the number of major faults equals the number of pages: one per page for the first touch, none afterwards. When it exceeds the limit (48 and 64 MiB) the kernel evicts pages that are needed again, and the counts jump to 60,595 and 120,062 faults, which is 4.9 and 7.3 times the number of pages (12,288 and 16,384). The run time rises from 0.07 s to 0.57 s. Because the storage of the build machine is fast and cached by the host, the slowdown is only a factor of eight; on a network disk or a rotating disk each major fault costs milliseconds and the same pattern produces a standstill.

blocks.text: The pressure stall information of the kernel recorded the episode. The counters in `/proc/pressure/memory` are cumulative microseconds during which tasks were stalled on memory.

blocks.code:
$ cat /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=0.00 avg60=0.05 avg300=0.35 total=3063149
full avg10=0.00 avg60=0.00 avg300=0.00 total=163924
$ ./thrash 64
working set  64 MiB: 300000 random reads in   0.43 s, major faults 120576, minor     75
$ cat /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=0.00 avg60=0.05 avg300=0.35 total=3148784
full avg10=0.00 avg60=0.00 avg300=0.00 total=249024
blocks.title: Pressure stall information before and after the 64 MiB run (typical output)

blocks.text:
During a run of 0.43 s the `some` total grew by 85.6 ms and the `full` total by 85.1 ms. `some` is the time at least one task was stalled on memory; `full` is the time all non-idle tasks were stalled at once. (The averages did not change visibly because the episode was shorter than the 10 second window.) PSI is the most direct indicator of memory pressure available on a modern kernel.

#### Swap configuration of the machine

blocks.code:
$ swapon --show; cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
60
blocks.title: Swap and swappiness on the build machine

blocks.text:
`swapon --show` prints nothing: no swap is configured on the build machine. All reclaim therefore concerns file pages, and anonymous memory is protected only by the OOM killer (see the chapter on memory limits and the OOM killer).

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: thrashing after a traffic increase

**Scenario.** A batch of report-generation jobs shares a 16 GiB virtual machine with a Spring Boot service. A new report type loads a larger data set, and the combined working sets of the service and the jobs exceed physical memory. The machine has a 4 GiB swap partition.

**Symptoms.** Response times rise from milliseconds to tens of seconds. Load average grows far above the CPU count while CPU utilisation is low. Disk reads and writes are high even though the application performs little I/O. `ssh` is sluggish.

**Diagnosis.** The commands are run in the order below. The output shown is typical for this condition (the build machine has no swap and cannot reproduce a swap storm; the page-fault and pressure mechanism was reproduced above).

blocks.title: Typical diagnosis of a swap storm (illustrative values)

blocks.text:
Reading the output: `b = 18` tasks are in uninterruptible sleep (waiting for I/O); `si` and `so` (4,180 and 5,320 KiB per second) show continuous swap-in and swap-out; `swpd` is almost the whole swap space; `free` and `cache` are tiny, so the page cache cannot absorb the load; `wa` (I/O wait) is 78 to 81 percent; PSI `full` of 71 percent means that for most of the time all non-idle tasks were stalled on memory. Together these identify thrashing, not a CPU or disk hardware problem. `ps -eo pid,rss,comm --sort=-rss | head` then names the processes with the largest resident sets.

**Root cause.** The sum of the working sets exceeds RAM, the scheduler keeps all processes runnable, and each fault evicts a page needed by another process.

**Fix.** Immediate: stop or pause the report jobs (`kill -STOP PID` freezes a process and lets its pages be reclaimed without further faults; `kill -CONT` resumes it), or restart the service with a smaller heap. Permanent: separate the batch workload from the service (different hosts or cgroups with `memory.high` and `memory.max`), size the heap so that heap, metaspace, stacks and the page cache working set fit, and set `-Xmx` below the memory the host can provide.

**Prevention.** Alert on PSI `full` above a few percent for a sustained period, on `si/so` greater than zero for more than a minute, and on the major fault rate. Run batch work under cgroup limits so that it is reclaimed before the service is.

#### Incident: garbage-collection pauses caused by swapped-out heap

**Scenario.** A Java service with a 6 GiB heap runs on a host with swap enabled and `vm.swappiness = 60`. Overnight the service is idle and a backup job reads large files. In the morning the first requests trigger a full collection.

**Symptoms.** The first full GC takes 40 seconds instead of 2 seconds. GC logs show a large difference between real time and CPU time (`real` much greater than `user + sys`). `vmstat` shows `si` high during the pause.

**Diagnosis.** The swapped-out size of the process is read from its status and the pause is correlated with swap-in.

blocks.code:
$ grep -E "VmRSS|VmSwap" /proc/PID/status
VmRSS:    163188 kB
VmSwap:        0 kB
blocks.title: Check how much of the process is in swap (healthy JVM of the build machine, no swap present)

blocks.text:
On the affected host `VmSwap` was several gigabytes while `VmRSS` was small; a large `VmSwap` value confirms that heap pages were swapped out. A garbage collector reads every live object, so it touches every page of the heap and the kernel must read the swapped pages back one fault at a time.

**Root cause.** The page cache of the backup competed with the idle heap, and the kernel moved cold anonymous pages to swap to enlarge the cache. The collector then faulted them all back.

**Fix.** Immediate: `swapoff -a && swapon -a` (only when enough free memory exists) forces the pages back before traffic arrives. Permanent: lower `vm.swappiness` (for example 1 to 10) on hosts that run JVMs, or disable swap for the service cgroup with `memory.swappiness=0` (cgroup v1) or `memory.swap.max=0` (cgroup v2); lock the heap with `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` and size the heap to the working set; throttle the backup with `ionice` and `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`.

**Prevention.** Monitor `VmSwap` of the main process; alert when it is not zero for a latency-sensitive service. Review the swappiness value in the host image.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **State Belady's anomaly and name an algorithm that is immune.** For some reference strings FIFO produces more faults with more frames (string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: 9 faults with three frames, 10 with four). LRU and OPT are immune because they are stack algorithms.
2. **Why is LRU not implemented exactly?** It needs an ordering update on every reference, and the CPU does not trap ordinary accesses. Systems approximate LRU with the hardware accessed bit (clock, active/inactive lists).
3. **Describe the clock algorithm.** Pages form a circular list with a reference bit. The hand advances; a page with bit 1 has its bit cleared and is skipped, a page with bit 0 is evicted. The sweep approximates least recently used.
4. **What is the working set and how does it relate to thrashing?** The set of pages referenced in the last Δ references. If the combined working sets exceed memory, processes fault constantly and CPU utilisation collapses; this is thrashing.
5. **How do you detect thrashing on a Linux server?** High `b` and `wa` in `vmstat`, non-zero `si` and `so`, rising `pgmajfault`, high load with idle CPU, and `/proc/pressure/memory` showing high `some` and `full` values.
6. **What does** `vm.swappiness` **control?** The balance between reclaiming anonymous pages (swap) and file pages (cache drop). It is a preference, not a switch: 0 does not disable swap.
7. **Why do many container platforms disable swap?** A limit with swap hides memory exhaustion behind severe slowdowns and makes latency unpredictable; an OOM kill at the limit is a clear failure that the orchestrator can handle by restarting.
8. **What is direct reclaim and why does it matter?** The allocating thread reclaims memory itself when `kswapd` cannot keep up. It adds latency to the application's own allocation, which shows up as pauses and as `pgscan_direct` in `/proc/vmstat`.
9. **Does adding RAM always reduce page faults?** For stack algorithms such as LRU yes (never more); for FIFO not necessarily. In practice more memory lets the page cache hold more of the working set, so faults usually fall.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Replacement chooses which resident page to evict; the fault count depends on the algorithm and the access pattern.

- OPT is the unreachable optimum; LRU approximates it; FIFO can show Belady's anomaly (9 then 10 faults on the reference string above).
- Hardware reference bits enable clock and the active/inactive lists used by Linux.
- Thrashing occurs when the working sets exceed memory; measured here as 4,096 and 8,192 faults for fitting working sets against 60,595 and 120,062 beyond the limit.
- `vmstat` (`b`, `wa`, `si`, `so`), `pgmajfault` and PSI (`/proc/pressure/memory`) detect memory pressure.
- Swap trades OOM kills for slowdowns; tune `vm.swappiness` and cgroup swap limits for latency-sensitive Java services.

sections.title: The Page Cache and Memory Used for File I/O

blocks.text:
Disks are three to five orders of magnitude slower than memory. Linux hides this gap by keeping the contents of recently used files in otherwise idle RAM, the **page cache**. Every `read`, every `write` and every file-backed `mmap` passes through it. As a consequence, a Linux machine that has been running for a while shows almost no free memory, and an inexperienced reader of `free` concludes that memory is exhausted. This chapter explains what the cache holds, how data moves through it, how the fields of `free` and `/proc/meminfo` are to be read, and why the cache matters for Java services and containers.

### Concept and mechanism

#### What the page cache stores

The page cache holds pages of file data keyed by (inode, page index) and also the metadata of block devices (the former "buffers"). All processes share it: the second process that reads a file finds the pages the first one loaded. Since Linux 2.4 the former buffer cache is unified with the page cache: a block-device buffer is a page of the cache with attached buffer heads, and the `Buffers` field of `/proc/meminfo` counts the part that holds raw block-device data such as file-system metadata.

rows: The kernel copies from a cache page to the user buffer; a miss reads the page (with read-ahead) from the device first.
The kernel copies the user buffer into a cache page and marks it dirty; the call returns before any I/O happens.
The page table points directly at the cache page; no copy, no system call per access; a fault loads a missing page.
Bypasses the cache; the device transfers to and from the user buffer; the caller handles alignment and caching.
Forces the dirty pages of the file (and the journal) to the device and waits.

blocks.text:
#### Read-ahead

When the kernel detects sequential access it reads additional pages before they are requested. The default window starts small and grows up to the device read-ahead setting (`blockdev --getra`, typically 128 KiB). The measurement in the chapter on paging showed the effect: reading a cold 32 MiB file through `mmap` caused one major fault, not thousands, and a `pread` of 16 MiB left 17 MiB in the cache (below).

#### Dirty pages and writeback

A page that has been modified in memory and not yet written to the device is **dirty**. Kernel flusher threads write dirty pages back in three situations: the page has been dirty longer than `vm.dirty_expire_centisecs` (30 seconds here), the amount of dirty memory exceeds `vm.dirty_background_ratio` percent of the reclaimable memory (10 here), or an application calls `fsync`. If dirty memory reaches `vm.dirty_ratio` (20 here), the writing process itself is throttled and must help write back before it may dirty more pages. These percentages refer to available memory (free plus reclaimable), not to total RAM. The flusher wakes every `vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs` (5 seconds here).

blocks.code:
$ for f in dirty_ratio dirty_background_ratio dirty_expire_centisecs dirty_writeback_centisecs; do \
    echo "$f=$(cat /proc/sys/vm/$f)"; done
dirty_ratio=20
dirty_background_ratio=10
dirty_expire_centisecs=3000
dirty_writeback_centisecs=500
blocks.title: Writeback tunables of the build machine

blocks.text: The consequence for durability is that a successful `write` does not mean that the data is on the device. Between the write and the writeback the data exists only in RAM and is lost on a power failure or a kernel crash. The chapter on buffered I/O and durability in the storage part covers `fsync`, `fdatasync` and the log-structured systems that depend on them.

blocks.text:
#### Reclaim of cache pages

Clean cache pages are the cheapest memory to reclaim: the kernel simply drops them, and a later access reads them again. Dirty pages must be written first. Therefore memory used by the cache is "free in an emergency", with two exceptions. Pages of `tmpfs` and shared anonymous memory (`Shmem`) appear in the `Cached` field but cannot be dropped without swap. Pages that are mapped and actively used by processes are kept by the active list.

### Worked trace: reading the output of free

The following figures were taken from the build machine after the cache experiment described later. `free -m` prints mebibytes.

blocks.code:
$ free -m
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            8029         580        6959          14         714        7449
Swap:              0           0           0
$ grep -E "^(MemTotal|MemFree|MemAvailable|Buffers|Cached|Dirty|Shmem|AnonPages|Mapped):" \
    /proc/meminfo
MemTotal:        8222320 kB
MemFree:         7125860 kB
MemAvailable:    7627648 kB
Buffers:           13408 kB
Cached:           706036 kB
Dirty:                 0 kB
Shmem:             14684 kB
AnonPages:        296256 kB
Mapped:           196448 kB
blocks.title: free and /proc/meminfo (build machine, typical)

rows: `MemTotal` (8222320 kB = 8029 MiB): RAM usable by the kernel (hardware reservations excluded).
`MemFree`: pages that hold nothing at all. Unused memory is wasted, so this value is expected to be small on a busy host.
`Buffers + Cached + SReclaimable` (13408 + 706036 + slab 12468 kB, about 714 MiB): file data, block metadata and reclaimable kernel caches.
`Shmem`: tmpfs and shared memory (14 MiB); counted in `Cached` but not reclaimable without swap.

`total − available` in current procps-ng (older versions: `total − free − buff/cache`). It approximates memory that cannot be dropped without consequence: anonymous pages (`AnonPages`, 289 MiB), kernel stacks, unreclaimable slab and page tables.
`MemAvailable`: the kernel estimate of memory obtainable without swapping: free pages plus the reclaimable part of the cache, minus the watermarks that must be kept. Use this value, not `free`.
blocks.caption: Meaning of the fields.

blocks.alt: Fields of free -m (values from the build machine, MiB, typical) | total 8029 = 356 in use (total − free − buff/cache) + 714 buff/cache + 6959 free | 356 cache 714 free 6959 | procps-ng: used = total − available; available = MemAvailable | used 580 available 7449 = free 6959 + reclaimable cache and slab (about 490) | buff/cache = Buffers + Cached + SReclaimable; Shmem (tmpfs) is inside Cached but not reclaimable without swap | Low 'free' with high 'available' is normal: the kernel uses idle RAM as page cache | Alert on MemAvailable and on major faults or PSI, not on MemFree

blocks.text:
The columns do not add up to the total in current procps-ng: 580 (used) + 6959 (free) + 714 (buff/cache) = 8253, which exceeds 8029, because `used` is defined as `total − available` and the cache is partly counted in both `used` and `buff/cache`. Under the older definition, `total − free − buff/cache`, the used memory would be 356 MiB. For capacity decisions only `available` is needed.

### Hands-on: the cache in action

#### Which pages of a file are cached

The program `cached.c` writes a 64 MiB file, evicts it, reads part of it and asks the kernel which pages are resident with the system call `mincore`.

blocks.title: cached.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -o cached cached.c && ./cached
after writing 64 MiB:          16384 of 16384 pages in the page cache
after POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED:         0 of 16384 pages in the page cache
after reading the first 16 MiB:  4352 of 16384 pages in the page cache
blocks.title: Run cached.c (typical output)

blocks.text:
The written file stays completely in the cache. `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)` drops the clean pages. Reading 16 MiB (4,096 pages) leaves 4,352 pages resident: the extra 256 pages (1 MiB) are the read-ahead window beyond the last request.

#### Cost of a cold versus a warm read

The script reads a 128 MiB file after writing it, after evicting it and again, and reports the cache size and the time.

blocks.code:
$ bash pc.sh
after write+sync:        Cached 800 MiB   free=6577 buff/cache=821 available=7175
after eviction (fadvise): Cached 672 MiB   free=6707 buff/cache=690 available=7175
after cold read:         Cached 800 MiB   free=6580 buff/cache=818 available=7176   [.044624081 s]
after warm read:         Cached 800 MiB   free=6580 buff/cache=818 available=7177   [.021703637 s]
after rm:                Cached 673 MiB   free=6706 buff/cache=690 available=7175
blocks.title: Page cache effect on a 128 MiB file (measured, typical; the cache columns include other activity of the machine)

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `Cached` rises by 128 MiB after the write and falls by the same amount after the eviction. The `free` column falls and rises by the same 130 MiB, while `available` does not change at all (7175 to 7177 MiB): the cache is memory that remains available to applications.
- The cold read took 45 ms and the warm read 22 ms. The storage of the build machine is a virtual disk with host-side caching, which makes the cold read unusually fast (2.9 GB/s); on a physical SSD or a network volume the difference is one to three orders of magnitude.
- `rm` returns the pages immediately because the file no longer exists.

#### The cache inside a memory cgroup

Page-cache pages are charged to the memory cgroup of the process that first touched them. A limit therefore bounds the cache as well, and the kernel reclaims cache pages of the group when the limit is approached. A cgroup with a 64 MiB limit was used to write 40 MiB and then 150 MiB more.

blocks.code:
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=cg.bin bs=1M count=40; sync
$ grep -E "^(cache|rss|inactive_file) " memory.stat; cat memory.usage_in_bytes
cache 41947136
rss 286720
inactive_file 41947136
43864064
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=cg2.bin bs=1M count=150; sync
$ grep -E "^(cache|rss) " memory.stat; cat memory.usage_in_bytes; cat memory.failcnt
cache 62918656
rss 278528
65548288
130
blocks.title: Cache charged to a 64 MiB memory cgroup (cgroup v1; typical output)

blocks.text:
After the first write the usage was 41.9 MB of cache and only 0.29 MB of anonymous memory. After the second write, which exceeded the limit by 86 MiB, the usage stayed at 65.5 MB, the cache was held at 62.9 MB, `failcnt` counted 130 limit hits and no process was killed: the kernel reclaimed clean cache pages to make room. This explains two facts about containers. The `memory.usage_in_bytes` value (and Docker's reported memory usage) includes the cache and therefore approaches the limit on any container that does file I/O, without indicating a problem. Kubernetes monitors the **working set**, defined as usage minus inactive file pages, to separate reclaimable cache from memory in use.

#### Mapping files and the JVM

The JVM maps the JDK class image (`lib/modules`, 137 MiB), its own shared library and the class-data-sharing archive; these pages are part of the page cache and of the process resident set (`RssFile`, 23,600 kB in the run shown in the first chapter of this part), and they are shared by all JVMs on the host. Java applications can map files explicitly with `FileChannel.map`, which returns a `MappedByteBuffer` backed by cache pages; the data is then accessed without `read` calls and without a copy into the Java heap. A mapped page that is not cached costs a major fault inside what looks like an ordinary memory access, which is a frequent cause of unexplained pauses in programs using memory-mapped files, because a JVM safepoint cannot interrupt a thread that waits in a page fault.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: false alarm on low free memory

**Scenario.** An alert named "Memory exhausted" fires when `MemFree / MemTotal` is below 10 percent. A search service that reads large index files has been running for two weeks on a 16 GiB host.

**Symptoms.** The alert fires daily. `free` shows 300 MiB free. The service responds normally, no swapping occurs and there are no `OutOfMemoryError` messages or kernel OOM records.

**Diagnosis.** The three values are compared and the use of the cache is established.

blocks.code:
$ free -m | sed -n 1,2p
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            8029         580        6959          14         714        7449
$ vmstat 1 3 | tail -1 | awk '{print "si=" $7, "so=" $8, "bi=" $9}'
si=0 so=0 bi=0
$ head -1 /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=0.00 avg60=0.00 avg300=0.18 total=3157741
blocks.title: Distinguish a full cache from a lack of memory (values from the build machine)

blocks.text:
The build machine is idle and shows the normal pattern for a healthy host: `available` close to `total`, no swap activity (`si`, `so` zero) and PSI near zero. A host in the described state shows `free` near zero and `buff/cache` near 15 GiB, but the same healthy signs: `available` large, `si` and `so` zero, PSI averages close to zero. The memory is in use as cache and is returned on demand.

**Root cause.** The alert measures the wrong quantity. Unused memory is not a goal; the page cache is meant to fill all free memory.

**Fix.** Replace the rule with `MemAvailable / MemTotal` below 10 percent, combined with PSI `some avg60` above a threshold or a nonzero swap-in rate. In Prometheus node exporter terms: `node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes`, not `node_memory_MemFree_bytes`.

**Prevention.** Teach the three-column rule to the on-call team: low `free` with high `available` is normal; low `available` is the problem. Do not run `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` to "free memory": it discards useful cache, forces the next requests to read from disk and can create the latency problem that it was meant to prevent.

#### Incident: latency after a nightly batch evicts the cache

**Scenario.** A nightly job scans a 200 GiB data file with ordinary reads on the same 32 GiB host that serves a database-backed API whose hot data is 20 GiB. At 02:00 the job starts; at 02:30 the API latency doubles and remains high for an hour after the job ends.

**Symptoms.** The API's read latency rises; `pgmajfault` and disk read throughput rise during the job; disk reads remain high for some time after the job; no process memory changes.

**Diagnosis.** The cache content is compared before and after the job.

blocks.code:
$ grep -E "^(Cached|Active\(file\)|Inactive\(file\)):" /proc/meminfo
Cached:           706036 kB
Active(file):     157504 kB
Inactive(file):   547264 kB
$ grep pgmajfault /proc/vmstat
pgmajfault 446084
blocks.title: Fields to sample before, during and after the scan (values of the idle build machine)

blocks.text:
`pgmajfault` is cumulative: subtracting two samples taken a minute apart gives the major-fault rate. During the scan the `Inactive(file)` list receives the scanned pages and the hot pages of the database are pushed out; afterwards the API reads its own data from disk until the cache has been rebuilt, which appears as a sustained major-fault rate and disk reads without any change in process memory.

**Root cause.** A one-pass scan pollutes the shared page cache. The active/inactive lists of Linux protect pages that were referenced twice, but the database's pages are touched less often than the scan streams new ones, and under a tight memory budget they are evicted.

**Fix.** Immediate: stop the job or lower its priority. Permanent: run the job with `posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)` after each chunk, with `O_DIRECT`, with `nocache` or in a memory cgroup of its own (`memory.limit_in_bytes` at 2 GiB, so that its cache is confined), and with `ionice -c3`.

**Prevention.** Alert on the major fault rate and on the cache hit ratio of the database; schedule scans on replicas; keep the hot data set smaller than the memory that the cache may use.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is the page cache and why does Linux use all free memory for it?** A cache of file data in RAM, shared by all processes. Free memory has no value; filling it with recently used file data avoids disk reads, and clean pages can be dropped instantly when memory is needed.
2. **What is the difference between** `free` **and** `available` **in** `free`**?** `free` counts pages holding nothing. `available` estimates the memory that can be given to applications without swapping, including reclaimable cache. Capacity decisions use `available`.
3. **What is the difference between buffers and cache?** Cache holds file contents; buffers hold block-device metadata (superblocks, inode tables, directory blocks). Both are page-cache pages today; `free` reports their sum.
4. **What happens when a process calls** `write` **and returns? Is the data on disk?** No. The data is in a dirty cache page. The flusher writes it within about 30 seconds, or at once on `fsync`. A crash before that loses it.
5. **How does** `mmap` **of a file differ from** `read`**?** `mmap` maps the cache pages into the address space: no copy, no system call per access, page faults load the data. `read` copies the data into a user buffer on each call.
6. **When is** `drop_caches` **appropriate?** Almost never in production; it is a benchmarking and debugging tool for creating a cold-cache state. It removes useful pages and does not fix memory leaks.
7. **Does the page cache count against a container's memory limit?** Yes, charged to the cgroup that loaded the pages. The kernel reclaims clean cache before the limit is enforced by an OOM kill, so high usage from cache is normal; the working-set metric excludes the inactive part.
8. **Why can a mapped-file Java application show unexplained latency?** A page fault that needs I/O blocks the thread for the duration of the read, and the JVM cannot reach a safepoint while the thread is inside the fault.
9. **What are the effects of** `vm.dirty_ratio` **set too high or too low?** Too high allows large bursts of dirty data and long stalls when it is finally flushed and more data lost on a crash; too low throttles writers early and lowers write throughput.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The page cache stores file data in otherwise unused RAM and is shared by all processes.

- `read` copies out of the cache, `write` copies in and marks the page dirty, `mmap` maps the cache pages directly.
- Read `available`, not `free`: in the measurement `available` stayed at 7175 MiB while the cache gained and lost 128 MiB.
- Dirty pages are written back after 30 seconds, at the background ratio or by `fsync`; until then a crash loses them.
- The cache is charged to the memory cgroup; the measured cgroup stayed at its 64 MiB limit with 62.9 MB of cache and no OOM kill.
- Do not use `drop_caches` as a remedy; scans that pollute the cache are controlled with `fadvise`, `O_DIRECT`, ionice and cgroups.

sections.title: Memory Limits, Overcommit and the OOM Killer

blocks.text:
A computer has a finite amount of memory, but the kernel promises more than it has: processes reserve address space that is never used, `fork` duplicates address spaces lazily, and sparse data structures touch only part of what they allocate. If every promise had to be backed by memory at the moment it was made, most programs could not run. Linux therefore **overcommits**. When the promises are called in, and no memory can be reclaimed, the kernel has one remaining option: kill a process. This chapter describes the policies that control overcommit, the selection logic of the OOM killer, the report that it writes, the difference between a global and a cgroup OOM, and the way these mechanisms appear in Java services on Kubernetes.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Overcommit modes

The sysctl `vm.overcommit_memory` selects how the kernel answers requests for address space (`malloc`, `mmap`, `brk`, `fork`).

rows: Heuristic: refuse a single request that is obviously larger than the total RAM plus swap
Allocations normally succeed; the shortage shows up later as an OOM kill
Maximum flexibility; `fork` of large processes never fails; OOM kills are the only limit
Strict: refuse when `Committed_AS` would exceed `CommitLimit` (swap + `vm.overcommit_ratio` percent of RAM, default 50)
`malloc` returns `NULL` instead of an OOM kill; large heaps may fail to start
blocks.caption: Overcommit policies.

blocks.text: `Committed_AS` in `/proc/meminfo` is the sum of the private writable address space that could be touched; `CommitLimit` is the ceiling used in mode 2. In mode 0 only the check for a single huge request applies. The program `overcommit.c` requests blocks of 1, 4, 16 and 64 GiB and never writes to them.

blocks.title: overcommit.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -o overcommit overcommit.c && ./overcommit
start                  Committed_AS:    1118592 kB
malloc( 1 GiB) -> success
after malloc           Committed_AS:    2167172 kB
malloc( 4 GiB) -> success
after malloc           Committed_AS:    6361480 kB
malloc(16 GiB) -> NULL
malloc(64 GiB) -> NULL
$ grep -E "CommitLimit|MemTotal" /proc/meminfo; cat /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory
MemTotal:        8222320 kB
CommitLimit:     4111160 kB
0
blocks.title: Run overcommit.c on the 8 GiB build machine (mode 0)

blocks.text: What to notice: a 4 GiB request succeeded although only 8 GiB of RAM exist and 1 GiB was already committed, because heuristic mode refuses only requests that alone exceed the RAM plus swap; the 16 GiB request failed. `Committed_AS` grew by the size of each granted block (1 GiB, then 4 GiB) while the resident memory of the process did not change at all, because no page was touched. The printed `CommitLimit` of 4,111,160 kB (50 percent of `MemTotal`, no swap) is not enforced in mode 0; it would be the ceiling in mode 2.

blocks.text:
#### When memory is really exhausted

Allocation of a physical page fails only when a process touches memory and no free page exists after reclaim. The kernel then runs the **OOM killer** (`out_of_memory()`), which chooses a victim, sends it `SIGKILL` and waits for its memory to be freed. Two kinds of OOM exist.

- **Global OOM**: the machine as a whole has no reclaimable memory. Any process may be chosen.
- **Memory cgroup OOM**: a cgroup reached its `memory.limit_in_bytes` (cgroup v1) or `memory.max` (cgroup v2) and reclaim within the group failed. Only processes of that cgroup are candidates, and the rest of the machine is not affected. This is the mechanism behind a container limit.

#### Selecting the victim

For each candidate task the kernel computes a **badness** value: the resident pages, the swap pages and the page-table pages of the task, scaled to a range of 0 to 1000 relative to the memory that is available to it (the machine, or the cgroup limit), plus the value `oom_score_adj` of the task (range -1000 to +1000). A value of -1000 exempts a task entirely; +1000 makes it the first choice. The task with the highest value is killed; the kernel prefers to kill a child with a nonzero badness before the parent. Kernel threads and PID 1 of the machine are never selected. The current values are visible per process:

rows: The badness value that the kernel would use now.
Adjustment from -1000 to 1000, inherited by children. Lowering it below its initial value needs the capability `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE`.
